narrative:
Saltmarsh Environmental Partners is a five-person environmental
consultancy on a tidal estuary, founded in 2011. Its clients are a port
authority, a county conservation district, and private landowners who
need a wetland line drawn before they can build. The work is field-heavy:
delineations, Phase I assessments, sediment sampling, and the long tail
of monitoring that a restoration permit requires.

The documents reflect a firm that lives between a field notebook and a
regulator. Scopes of work go out as letters and come back countersigned
and scanned. Sampling programs produce data workbooks whose totals the
Managing Principal checks before anything is submitted. Monitoring
reports are written for an agency reviewer who will read them years
later, so they say what was measured, where, and on what date, and they
do not editorialize.

Tone is plain, technical, and careful. Scientists write in the passive
where the method matters and the actor does not. Nobody oversells a
finding; a hedge is a professional obligation here, not a weakness. Staff
use first names internally and full names with an agency on the page. One
long-standing client contact moved from the conservation district to the
port authority mid-history, and the documents should show it: the same
person, the correct employer for the date on the page.
instructions:
Author every document briefed in `docs`, as JSON matching the deliverable
schema:

  {"schema_id": "orgsmith/authoring-deliverable@1",
   "work_order_id": "wo:author:0002",
   "docs": [{"schema_id": "orgsmith/docir@1", "doc_id": "d:....",
             "blocks": [...]}, ...]}

Block kinds: heading (text, level), paragraph (text), list (items),
table (header, rows), sigblock (signers = person ids from the brief).

Hard rules:
- One DocIR per brief; doc_ids must match the work order exactly.
- Every fact id briefed for a doc MUST appear as a literal placeholder
  {{fact:<id>}} at least once in that doc's text, where <id> is the
  briefed id verbatim including its `f:` prefix (e.g.
  {{fact:f:E-2019-001.start}}). You do not know fact values; never write
  a number, date, or name in place of a placeholder.
- Use only placeholders for fact ids briefed on that document.
- Do not invent people, organizations, addresses, amounts, or dates.
  People and their titles come from the briefs; the org narrative sets
  tone only.
- Every entry in a doc's `mentions` list must appear VERBATIM (the exact
  `surface` string) somewhere in that doc's text. Sigblock signers count
  as mentions of themselves. Short surfaces are nicknames: work them into
  prose naturally ("...as {{nickname}} noted..."), alongside, not instead
  of, the person's full name.
- If a doc carries `engagement_position`, honor it: it states where the
  document sits in its engagement's timeline. Do not describe progress or a
  phase inconsistent with it, and do not state the engagement's start or
  end date (those are fact placeholders, not yours to write).
- If a doc carries `firm_digest`, it is the ONLY firm history you may treat
  as established as of this document's date. Reference clients only through
  the placeholders it names; claim no engagement it does not list; present
  nothing later than this document as already true.
- If a doc carries `reporting_line`, the person reports to exactly who it
  names and to no one else. Do not name any other person or title as their
  supervisor; a reporting relationship is owned by the ledger, not invented.
- Write plain, era-appropriate business prose in the org's voice.

authors.name: Angela Flynn
authors.title: Managing Principal
authors.persona: The firm's final reader. Angela signs the scopes that leave the office and checks every workbook total herself before a submission reaches an agency, on the principle that a number she has not verified is a number she cannot defend. Her prose is spare and unhurried; she will hedge a finding on purpose and treats the hedge as part of the work, not a softening of it.

participants.name: Angela Williams
participants.title: Field Technician
participants.persona: Angela came up through the field before she moved to the desk, and it shows in how she reports: she trusts what she has seen at the flag line over what a map suggests. She is at home in wetland vegetation and sediment work and writes with the economy of someone who has taken the reading herself in the marsh. She goes by her first name with colleagues and uses her full name on anything an agency will read.

participants.name: Mary Foster
participants.title: Field Technician
participants.persona: Mary is a sampler's sampler, steady with sediment cores and the labeling discipline that keeps a data workbook honest. She writes field notes, not prose, and they are exact: station, depth, condition, time. What she records in the marsh is what the report is built on, and she treats that responsibility literally.

participants.name: John Sanchez
participants.title: Senior Scientist
participants.persona: John runs the technical side of the fieldwork and is the one who turns a season of field notes into a monitoring report a reviewer can follow long after the fact. He writes plainly and in the passive where the method carries the weight, naming what was measured, where, and when, and letting the actor disappear. Careful to a fault, he would rather qualify a conclusion than reach past his data.

docs.guidance: Formal engagement letter on firm letterhead confirming the engagement. Do NOT repeat the firm's name as a heading or title line: the letterhead already carries it. Open with the client's inside address and a salutation, then cover scope and approach, the team, and the fee and start date, followed by the standard terms a real engagement letter carries -- each as its own short headed paragraph: fees and payment, term and termination, confidentiality, limitation of liability, and governing law. Close with a signature request and end with a sigblock block signed by the letter's author and the client contact. Commercial fee terms are executed on the signature page by counsel; do not state, estimate, or reference the fee amount anywhere in the text. Write in a plainspoken, direct register: concrete nouns and verbs, no epigrams or aphorisms. Vary your openings, section names, and closings from what a template would produce. Do not open with 'Two asks. First... Second...'; do not structure the document as 'Workstreams' then 'Next Steps' then a closing aphorism; and avoid the 'rather X now than Y later' antithesis and formulaic epigrams. Your personal writing style, held consistently: a plainspoken register (concrete nouns and verbs, no epigrams) in medium sentences. You habitually: avoids lists entirely and writes in paragraphs; sets context in a sentence before making any request. Never use 'In short,' as a paragraph opener; a 'Workstreams' heading followed by 'Next Steps'.
